summary: A hierarchy opened level by level — folders, an org chart, nested categories. One tab stop, arrow keys inside, only open rows rendered; selectable one or many.
useWhen: the data is a hierarchy of unknown depth and the user needs to see where an item sits in it — a folder of knowledge files, teams within departments
people pick one node, or several, from that hierarchy — a destination folder, the sources an agent may read
the hierarchy is too large to show open, so levels open on demand

useInstead.when: the hierarchy is the app's own pages — navigation
useInstead.why: navigation is links reached by Tab, with `aria-current`. A tree is one tab stop with arrow keys inside, which hides every page from Tab and is announced as data, not as navigation

useInstead.when: there are two levels and the second is short — sections of settings, FAQ groups
useInstead.why: a tree's keyboard model is overhead for a list of headings with content under each

useInstead.when: the rows have columns — size, owner, modified
useInstead.why: TreeView is a single-column treegrid; nested rows with columns are a table's job

useInstead.when: the items are flat — records to open or pick, with no nesting
useInstead.why: a tree's levels and expand keys are overhead when there is nothing to open

useInstead.when: picking several values from a flat list

requires: `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` — the tree's name, such as "Knowledge files"
a unique `id` on every item across the whole tree — keys are how selection and expansion are held
a string `label`, or `textValue` when the label is not text — typeahead matches it and it is the row's name
guarantees: a `treegrid` of flat rows, each with `aria-level`, `aria-posinset` and `aria-setsize` among its siblings, and `aria-expanded` only on rows that have children
one tab stop: ↑ and ↓ move between visible rows, → opens a row, ← closes it or moves to its parent, Home and End go to the ends, and typing jumps to a matching label
only open rows are rendered, so a closed branch cannot be landed on
each parent's chevron is a button named "Expand" or "Collapse" in the user's locale, out of the tab order, and opens the row without selecting it
`selectionMode="multiple"` sets `aria-multiselectable` and draws a check in every row; the row's `aria-selected` is the announcement
a disabled item is skipped by the arrow keys and cannot be selected
`description` is read as the row's description
every level indents by spacing/20, from the right in a right-to-left locale, where ← opens
rows are at least 32px tall with a 24px chevron target; the keyboard focus ring is drawn on the row
notes: → on a row that is already open stays on it: in a treegrid → moves into a row's own cells, not its children. ↓ goes on to the first child
selection does not cascade: selecting a parent selects that item only. A permissions tree where a parent means "all of these" needs the caller to expand the selection

`onAction` fires on Enter, and on a press when nothing is selectable — for "open this": show the file, go to the folder. With `selectionMode="none"` and no `onAction`, a press on a parent opens or closes it

antiPatterns.dont: <TreeView items={pages} onAction={navigate} /> for the app's own sections
antiPatterns.why: pages in a tree are hidden from Tab and read as data; Sidebar's rows are links

antiPatterns.dont: a tree of nested Accordions or indented Checkboxes
antiPatterns.why: nested accordions are a tab stop per heading, and indented checkboxes carry no level — a screen reader hears a flat list

antiPatterns.dont: ids that repeat under different parents — two "docs" folders with id "docs"
antiPatterns.do: ids from the path or the record — "policies/docs", "fld_812"
antiPatterns.why: expansion and selection are held by id, so two rows with one id open, close and select together

antiPatterns.dont: rendering every level open to show the whole hierarchy
antiPatterns.do: `defaultExpandedKeys` for the path to what matters, the rest closed
antiPatterns.why: a tree opened in full is a long flat list with indentation, and loses the one thing a tree gives: seeing the shape before the detail
